pages.md:
The **Sandboxed plugins** section of the Plugin Gallery lists plugins from a
static registry that ships with Lumen. There is no plugin server: the registry
is a folder of files, and every version in it passes the safety scan before it
is listed.

## The ten plugins

These are modelled on the kinds of Obsidian plugins people download most
(templates, task boards, calendars, tables, linting, tags, spaced repetition,
refactoring, dates, sorting). Each is written for Lumen's sandbox: none of them
uses the network, so they all work under the **local-only** AI policy.

| Plugin | What it does | Permissions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Templates** | Inserts a note from your `Templates` folder, filling `{{date}}`, `{{date:DD/MM/YYYY}}`, `{{time}}`, `{{title}}`, `{{selection}}`, `{{weekday}}` and `{{hebrewWeekday}}`. | commands, read the vault, read and change the open note, panel, settings |
| **Kanban board** | Draws a ` ```kanban ` block (a `## heading` per column, a `- item` per card) as columns, and copies the board as a Markdown table. | code-block renderer, commands, read and change the open note, clipboard, notifications |
| **Calendar** | A month view of your daily notes (`YYYY-MM-DD.md`). Days that have a note link to it. The week starts on Sunday, or on Monday if you choose. | commands, panel, read the vault, settings |
| **Table formatter** | Lines up the columns of every table and sorts a table by the column under the cursor. Hebrew niqqud takes no width. | commands, read and change the open note |
| **Markdown tidy** | Fixes trailing spaces, extra blank lines, heading spacing, mixed bullets and a missing final newline. It never touches code or front matter. | commands, read and change the open note, notifications, settings |
| **Tag manager** | Lists every `#tag` in the vault, Hebrew tags included, and renames a tag and its nested tags everywhere at once. | commands, panel, read and change the vault, notifications |
| **Flashcards** | Turns `question :: answer` lines into cards and schedules reviews with SM-2. The note itself is never changed. | commands, read the open note, panel, storage |
| **Note refactor** | Moves the selection into a new note and leaves a `[[link]]` in its place, or splits a note into one note per heading. | commands, read and change the open note, read and change the vault, notifications, settings |
| **Natural dates** | Turns “tomorrow”, “next Friday”, “in 3 days”, “מחר”, “יום שישי הבא” or 12/11/2026 (day first) into `[[2026-11-13]]`. | commands, read and change the open note, notifications, settings |
| **Sort lines** | Sorts the selected lines A→Z, Z→A or by length, reverses them, or removes duplicates. Sub-items stay with their item. Hebrew sorts by letter (final letters sort with their regular forms), and numbers sort by value. | commands, read and change the open note, notifications |

Install one from **Plugin Gallery → Sandboxed plugins → Install…**. The
permission screen lists everything the plugin asks for and why. Once a plugin is
installed, its card shows **Remove**, which stops the plugin and deletes the
settings and data it stored.

The plugins write their labels in English and Hebrew, because the plugin API
does not tell a plugin which language the app is in.

## How the registry is built

```
public/plugins/examples/
  index.json          ← built: every plugin, its versions, the SHA-256 of each version's code and manifest
  index.json.sig      ← the owner's Ed25519 signature over index.json (written by --sign)
  scan.json           ← built: the safety scan of every version
  kanban/             ← one folder per version
    lumen-plugin.json
    main.js
```

```sh
node scripts/build-plugin-registry.mjs           # rebuild index.json and scan.json
node scripts/build-plugin-registry.mjs --check   # fail if either is out of date, a version fails, or index.json.sig no longer matches
```

The build does the following:

- validates every manifest;
- refuses stray files in a plugin folder (only the manifest, its entries, a `LICENSE` and a `README` are allowed);
- refuses an id and version that appear twice;
- writes `index.json`;
- scans every version (`scripts/scan-plugins.mjs`).

A new version goes in a folder of its own, for example `kanban@1.1.0`.

When you install a plugin, the app scans the downloaded code again. It refuses
the code if its SHA-256 differs from the hash in the registry scan.

## The signed registry

The owner signs the exact bytes of `index.json` with an Ed25519 key that stays
on the owner's machine. Because `index.json` lists the SHA-256 of every
version's code and manifest, that one signature covers every file a user can
install.

```sh
node scripts/build-plugin-registry.mjs --keygen ~/keys      # once: a new key; prints the VITE_PLUGIN_TRUSTED_KEYS value
LUMEN_PLUGIN_SIGNING_KEY=~/keys/lumen-plugin-registry.pem node scripts/build-plugin-registry.mjs --sign
```

Set the printed `VITE_PLUGIN_TRUSTED_KEYS` in the build's environment. The app
trusts only that key, or a key you trusted yourself under Settings. The public
key written in `index.json.sig` is never trusted on its own.

When a folder has `index.json.sig`, **Install** takes the signed path
(`src/plugins/install.ts`), and each step can refuse the install:

1. `index.json` and `index.json.sig` are downloaded. The downloads are listed
   in the privacy ledger.
2. The signature over `index.json` must verify against a trusted key. One
   changed byte anywhere in `index.json` fails here.
3. The manifest and the code are downloaded, and each SHA-256 must match the
   signed `index.json`.
4. The code is scanned. Then it runs in its QuickJS sandbox with the
   permissions the manifest declares, as listed on the permission screen.

**Remove** stops the sandbox, deletes what the plugin stored and deletes its
install record and permissions.

A registry from another site is installed only through this path, and an
unsigned one is refused. Only the folder that ships with the app
(`/plugins/examples`), served from the app's own origin, falls back to the
SHA-256 check against its scan when it has no `index.json.sig`.

## Themes tested in RTL (W12.S6)

Every theme in the gallery (`public/themes/examples/`) is reviewed like a
plugin version with only a stylesheet (the review on the
[Security](/security/) page: licence, public source, no remote CSS), and then
checked for right-to-left use. `node scripts/themes/rtl-check.mjs` writes its
scorecard to `public/themes/examples/scorecards/<id>@<version>.json`;
`--check` fails when one is stale, and `--css <file>` checks one stylesheet.

- **Physical CSS.** `margin-left`, `padding-right`, `left:`/`right:`,
  one-sided borders and corners, `float`, `clear` and `text-align` with
  `left`/`right` break a Hebrew layout. Each one is reported with the
  logical property to use instead (`margin-inline-start`, `text-align:
  start`, …). A rule scoped to one direction (`[dir="rtl"] …`, `:dir(ltr)`)
  is allowed.
- **Contrast** (WCAG 2.2, 1.4.3): the theme's text colours against its
  backgrounds, 4.5:1, in light and in dark. The app's own colours fill in
  whatever the theme leaves unset.
- **Screens.** Eight screens (editor, preview, table, lists, callouts, code
  inside Hebrew, Bases, settings) are captured in RTL and in LTR by a
  browser run, merged with `--screens <results.json>`.

A failing RTL check is a warning on the scorecard, not a delisting: each
finding costs the score what any review warning costs (10 points). The
**Tested in RTL** badge is given only when all three pass, so it waits for
the browser run. There are no user ratings: ratings need accounts and
moderation, and the scorecard and the badge do that job.

## A registry site of its own

The same registry can be published as a static site of its own on Cloudflare
Pages, the second host. A developer outside the project can then get a plugin
listed with a pull request, without waiting for an app release.

```sh
npm run registry:site                 # builds dist-registry/ (it first checks that index.json and scan.json are current)
npm run registry:verify -- dist-registry
npx wrangler pages deploy dist-registry --project-name lumen-md-plugins --branch main
npm run registry:verify -- https://lumen-md-plugins.pages.dev
```

The site holds:

- `v1/index.json`: every plugin and every version that passed its scan, with
  its permissions, its scan grade and findings, and the SHA-256 and size of
  each file. A version that failed its scan is left out.
- `v1/plugins/<id>/<version>/`: the files. They are served as text and never
  rewritten, so they can be cached forever.
- `SHA256SUMS`, in the format `sha256sum -c` reads.
- `index.html`: the list, in Hebrew and English, with no scripts.
- `_headers`: `nosniff`, read-only CORS, and a CSP that allows nothing to run.

`registry:verify` recomputes every hash and **scans every version again**
on your machine. A host that changed a file, or that lists a version the scan
would refuse, fails the check. The site fits the free plan with room to
spare: 40 files of the 20,000 allowed, 4 header rules of the 100 allowed.

The app still reads the registry it ships (`/plugins/examples`). Reading this
site from the app is a separate step, because the app's CSP would need its
address.

## Not yet

- The registry that ships with the app is **not signed yet**: signing it needs
  the owner's key (`--keygen`, then `--sign`, above), so its cards still show
  the “unsigned” note. See also [Plugin signing keys](/plugins/signing/).
- The registry site (`npm run registry:site`) does not publish `index.json.sig`
  yet, and the app does not read that site yet.

pages.title: Plugin sandbox and permissions
pages.description: How Lumen runs plugins with no access by default — QuickJS for logic, UI as data, a capability list the user grants.
pages.md:
Lumen runs every plugin with **no access by default**. A plugin gets only
the capabilities you grant it when you install it, and you can revoke them
at any time.

## Where plugin code runs

| Part | Runs in | What it can reach |
|---|---|---|
| Logic (`main`) | [QuickJS](https://github.com/justjake/quickjs-emscripten) (MIT), a separate JavaScript engine compiled to WebAssembly, inside its own Web Worker | Only the `lumen` object. There is no `fetch`, `XMLHttpRequest`, `WebSocket`, `importScripts`, DOM or storage, and no `import` of other modules. |
| Interface (panels, settings, block output) | Lumen itself | The plugin sends a **tree of known elements**: text, heading, paragraph, box, list, button, input, checkbox, select, code, link to a note, divider. There is no `img`, `iframe`, `form`, `style`, `script` or HTML, and no link to a web address. |

The interface is data rather than a sandboxed iframe on purpose. CSP and the
iframe `sandbox` attribute block every channel but one: a frame may always
navigate *itself* (`location = "https://…?" + text`). A tree of known
elements has no such channel.

## Limits

Each plugin has a 32 MB heap and a 512 KB stack. It gets 250 ms of CPU each
time Lumen enters its code (an event, the reply to a call), and its console
is capped at 120 lines a minute. A plugin that goes over a limit, or throws
an error nobody catches, is stopped.

## Capabilities

| Capability | Gives |
|---|---|
| `document:read` / `document:write` | The open note's text and selection / changing it |
| `vault:read` / `vault:write` | Listing and reading notes / writing notes |
| `commands` | Commands in the palette |
| `panel` | A side panel |
| `renderer` | Rendering a code-block language |
| `settings` | A settings section |
| `storage` | Its own key–value storage |
| `clipboard:write` | Copying text |
| `notifications` | Toasts |
| `network:https://exact.origin` | Requests to **that origin only** — https (http only for localhost), no cookies, no redirects, at most 5 MB of response |

Every capability the manifest asks for comes with a reason, which is shown
to you before you grant it. A call without its capability fails inside the
plugin with `PluginDenied` and never reaches Lumen. Lumen checks the grant
a second time on the host side, because the worker is a boundary, not the
policy.

## Network and privacy

Every request a plugin makes appears in the **privacy ledger** under
"Plugin". Under the **local-only** AI policy, plugin requests are blocked
and logged as blocked, even when the plugin has a network grant.

## Manifest (`lumen-plugin.json`)

```json
{
  "schema": 1,
  "id": "org.example.word-stats",
  "name": "Word stats",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "description": "Counts words in the open note",
  "author": "Example",
  "license": "MIT",
  "main": "main.js",
  "capabilities": [
    { "id": "document:read", "reason": "To count the words of the open note" },
    { "id": "commands", "reason": "Adds the “Word stats” command" }
  ]
}
```

{c} 📊
{c}
); } ``` That's the whole plugin. ` ```emoji-csv ` blocks now render with the emoji headers everywhere Lumen renders markdown.

pages.md:
Registry plugins can be signed with an **Ed25519** key. Before installing,
Lumen verifies the signature against the keys you trust, so a compromised
CDN cannot ship modified code.

## Manage trusted keys

Command palette → **Trusted plugin signing keys…**

- **Built-in** keys come from the deployment (`VITE_PLUGIN_TRUSTED_KEYS`)
  and cannot be removed from the UI.
- **Your keys** are stored in this browser. Paste the publisher's public key
  and press **Trust key**.

Each key is identified by its **fingerprint** — the SHA-256 of the public
key, in hex. Compare it with the fingerprint the publisher lists on their
website before trusting it.

## Accepted formats

- Base64 SPKI (44 bytes for Ed25519, starts with `MCow`).
- PEM: `-----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY----- … -----END PUBLIC KEY-----`.

Generate a key pair with OpenSSL:

```bash
openssl genpkey -algorithm ed25519 -out plugin-signing.pem
openssl pkey -in plugin-signing.pem -pubout
```

## Errors

- **Not an Ed25519 public key** — the pasted text is not a 44-byte SPKI
  Ed25519 key (RSA and ECDSA keys are not accepted).
- **Untrusted signer** — the plugin is correctly signed, but by a key you
  have not trusted. Verify the fingerprint, then add the key.

pages.description: Start a note from a template — the built-in ones, the gallery, and the ones you install — and where an installed template lives.
pages.md:
## Start from a template

The command palette lists templates as commands. Pick one and it opens
as a **new, unsaved tab**: it never writes into the note you have open,
and a name that is already taken gets a number (*Meeting notes 2.md*).

## The template gallery

`⌘K → Browse template gallery` opens the gallery: filter by category,
search by name, and **Install** a template. Installing writes it to
`templates/<id>.md` in your vault and adds it to the palette under
**Templates: <name>**. It is an ordinary note, so you can edit it like
any other. With the interface in Hebrew, templates that have a Hebrew
version install in Hebrew.

The gallery's list ships with the app (`public/templates/registry.json`),
so browsing it makes no request to any other site.

## Adding a template to the gallery

See `public/templates/CONTRIBUTING.md` in the repository: one Markdown
file plus an entry in `registry.json` (and a Hebrew file under
`public/templates/he/` when there is one).
---
title: Templates and sample vaults
description: The template gallery, the twenty Israeli templates with their Bases views, placeholders, importing a template from a file, and the three sample vaults.
---

**⌘K → Browse template gallery** opens the gallery. **Install** copies a
template into your workspace as `templates/<id>.md`; from then on it is in
**⌘K → Templates**, and choosing it opens a new, unsaved note from it. The
gallery speaks the UI's language: in Hebrew you get the Hebrew name,
description and body of every template that has one.

## Templates for Israeli use cases

Twenty templates, each in Hebrew and in English:

| Area | Templates |
|---|---|
| Journal | Daily journal (with the Hebrew date), weekly review (Sunday–Thursday) |
| Student | University course (semester, credits), exam (Moed A / B), lecture summary, seminar paper |
| Research | Article to read, research log / experiment |
| Work | Team meeting, one-on-one, project (kanban), task |
| Home | Recipe (meat / dairy / pareve, Shabbat), holiday plan, apartment hunting (₪ rent, arnona, va'ad bayit) |
| Reading and writing | Book I'm reading, book chapter, character |
| Personal | Reserve duty (miluim) log, job application (kanban) |

Every one of them stores its facts as **properties** in the frontmatter, with
English keys (`type`, `status`, `due`…) and values in your language, so the
same note works in Lumen and in Obsidian.

### A Bases view with every template

Each template comes with a companion [`.base` file](/workspace/obsidian-bases/).
Installing the template also writes it to `Bases/` (for example
`Bases/Courses.base`, or `Bases/קורסים.base` in Hebrew): a table, cards or
kanban view of every note with that template's `type`, with column names in
your language. If the file is already there, it is left alone, so your
changes to the view survive a reinstall.

## Placeholders

When a template becomes a note, these are filled in — the same names as
Obsidian's core Templates plugin:

| Placeholder | Becomes |
|---|---|
| `{{title}}` | the note's name |
| `{{date}}` | today, `YYYY-MM-DD` |
| `{{time}}` | now, `HH:mm` |
| `{{hebrewDate}}` | today in the Hebrew calendar, for example `30 Heshvan 5787` |

Anything else in double braces is left as it is.

## Import a template from a file

**⌘K → Import template from file…**, or **Import from file…** at the top of
the gallery, copies a Markdown file you pick into `templates/`. A name that
is taken gets a number (`Recipe.md`, then `Recipe 2.md`), and characters that
can't be in a file name are replaced with spaces. The template is in
**⌘K → Templates** straight away.

## Sample vaults

Three ready-made vaults show the templates, links and Bases views working
together. Each opens from the command palette, in the UI's language, into a
folder of its own:

- **Open sample vault: student** — two courses, lecture summaries and an
  exam with a study plan; views of courses, lectures and exams.
- **Open sample vault: researcher** — a thesis, three articles and two
  experiments; views of the literature, the research log and the papers.
- **Open sample vault: writer** — three chapters and three characters,
  linked to each other; views of the manuscript and the characters.

Like the sample workspace, a sample vault never overwrites anything: running
it again only adds the files that are missing.

pages.title: Web Clipper
pages.description: Save a web page as a clean Markdown note, from inside Lumen or with the browser extension, which hands the clip to the app. No clip server.
pages.md:
## Clip from inside Lumen

Two commands save a page into your vault as a clean note, with its source
and the date in the front matter:

- `⌘K → Clip a web page…` — paste a URL; Lumen fetches the page and keeps
  the article (`<article>` / `<main>`), without navigation, ads, forms and
  scripts. Fetching an arbitrary site needs the research service
  ([Research](/ai/research/)); without it, only sites the app's security
  policy already allows can be clipped, and Lumen says so. Under the
  local-only AI policy, Lumen fetches no web pages at all; use
  **Clip from clipboard** instead.
- `⌘K → Clip from clipboard` — copy something on a page first; the copied
  HTML (or text) becomes the note.

Clips go into the **Library** folder (**ספרייה** with the interface in
Hebrew), get a number when the name is taken, and open in a new tab.

```yaml
---
title: "How CRDTs Work"
source: "https://martin.kleppmann.com/2020/07/06/crdt-hard-parts.html"
clipped: 2026-04-26
---
```

## The browser extension

The Lumen Web Clipper is a Chrome / Edge extension (Manifest V3). It sends
the page to Lumen, and **Lumen** turns it into a note. The extraction
happens in the app, so a clip comes out the same whichever way it arrives.

### Install (developer mode)

1. `chrome://extensions/` → turn on **Developer mode**
2. **Load unpacked** → pick the `extension/` folder of the repository
3. Open the extension's **Settings**: set the address of your Lumen (default
   `http://localhost:5173`), or choose **The Lumen desktop app**.

### Use

- **Save full page**: the toolbar button, or right-click → **Clip to Lumen**.
- **Save selection only**: select text first. Only the selection becomes the note.
- **Highlighter**: toolbar → **Highlighter on/off**, then select passages on
  the page. They are kept per address, marked again when you come back,
  and put at the top of the note (as `==highlight==` quotes) on the next clip.

### How a clip reaches Lumen

| Where Lumen runs | How |
|---|---|
| Browser tab | The extension finds (or opens) the Lumen tab and hands the clip to the page with `postMessage`. The app takes messages only from its own window and origin. |
| Desktop app | A `lumen://clip?…` link. If Lumen is already open, the running window gets it. |

Nothing is uploaded anywhere: there is no clip server.

## What a clip contains

The readable part of the page, found by [Defuddle](https://github.com/kepano/defuddle)
(MIT), with Mozilla Readability (Apache-2.0) as a fallback, and converted to
Markdown by Turndown (MIT):

```yaml
---
title: "The Counterpane"
source: "https://example.com/story"
author: "Ada Pierce"
published: "2026-10-01"
clipped: "2026-10-24"
tags: [clip]
---
```

Links and images point at the original page. Clips go into the library
folder (`Library/`, or `ספרייה/` when Lumen is in Hebrew).

### Templates by site

| Site | Folder | Extra |
|---|---|---|
| Wikipedia (any language) | `Library/Wikipedia` | `license: CC BY-SA 4.0`, `summary` |
| ynet | `Library/ynet` | `summary`, `topics`, `tags: [clip, news]` |
| Haaretz | `Library/Haaretz` | `summary`, `topics`, `tags: [clip, news]` |
| YouTube | `Library/YouTube` | `channel`, `published`, `summary`; the transcript when its panel is open |
| arXiv | `Library/arXiv` | `authors`, `arxiv`, `published`, `pdf`, `contribution`; the abstract |
| GitHub repositories | `Library/GitHub` | `description`, `purpose` |
| Pages marked as a schema.org `Recipe` | `Library/Recipes` | `tags: [clip, recipe]` |

A template is picked by its triggers: an address prefix, a `/regular expression/`
or `schema:@Type`. The first match wins.

Besides `{{title}}`, `{{url}}`, `{{content}}` and the rest, a template can read
the page with `{{meta:name}}` (a `<meta>` tag, by name, property or itemprop;
several tags of one name are joined) and `{{selector:css}}` (the text of the
elements a CSS selector picks).

### Your own templates

Run **Web clipper: templates and triggers** from the palette. Your templates
come first, before the built-in ones above, and are saved in the vault at
`.lumen/clip-templates.json`, so they sync with your notes. A built-in
template is read-only: *Duplicate* it to change it. *Test an address* shows
which template a page would get, and by which trigger. The preview shows the
note it makes from sample values. A trigger that is not an address, a valid
`/regex/` or `schema:@Type` is named before you can save. Templates exported
from the Obsidian Web Clipper (its JSON *Export*) can be imported as they are.

## Interpreter: fields a local model fills in

A template can ask questions about the page: `{{"a one-sentence summary"}}`,
`{{"three key topics"|lower}}`. When a clip uses such a template, Lumen asks a
**model on your own device** — Ollama on this computer or your local network,
or the in-browser model if it is already loaded — and writes the answers into
the note. There is no cloud route: under any AI policy, the interpreter never
sends a page to an AI provider. With no local model running, those fields are
left out and the clip is saved as usual.

- The model reads only what the template points at (its `context` selectors:
  the abstract on arXiv, the lead section on Wikipedia, the transcript on
  YouTube), cut to about 6 000 characters, so a small model's window is
  enough. No `OLLAMA_ORIGINS` or context-size setting is needed in the
  desktop app.
- All questions of a template go in one request.
- The page text passes the prompt-injection guard before the model sees it,
  marked as outside data, and every answer is checked again before it is
  written into the note.

## Safety

A clip is outside content. Its `source:` marks the note as untrusted for the
AI agents (plan 2.7). Before the
note is saved, hidden text (zero-width characters, invisible tag characters,
hidden HTML) and instruction-like passages ("ignore previous instructions…")
are removed or visibly marked, with a warning at the top of the note.

## Accuracy

On the clipper golden set (plan 7.10: 20 pages with ads, cookie banners,
share bars, comments and footers around a public-domain article), the clip
must have the exact title, every paragraph in order and no noise on at least
90 % of pages. This is checked on every change (`clipperGolden.test.ts`).

## Privacy

The in-app commands fetch only the page you ask for (through the research
service when one is set up). The extension sends nothing over the network:
it reads the page you clip and hands it to your Lumen tab (`postMessage`) or
to the desktop app (a `lumen://clip` link). Its only request is opening your
Lumen address when no Lumen tab is open. No tracking and no telemetry. Its
manifest is
[`extension/manifest.json`](https://github.com/talstilkol/lumen-md/blob/main/extension/manifest.json).

pages.title: The beta programme
pages.description: Join the beta from inside Lumen, send feedback as a prefilled GitHub issue, and — only if you ask — a weekly report of counts. Nothing leaves without your click.
pages.md:
The beta programme gives you new features first, and gives the project
what it needs most: people who write in Hebrew using Lumen for real.

## Join from the app

Command palette → **Help: Beta programme**, then tick **Join the beta on
this device**. Joining does three things, all on this device:

- **Beta features on.** Every feature still in beta is turned on here, as
  if you had switched each one on in **Feature flags…**.
- **Beta updates (desktop app).** The update channel becomes *beta*, so the
  app installs beta releases too. It reads the release pipeline's
  `beta-channel` pointer on GitHub Releases. The web beta is a separate site;
  see [Beta channel and feature flags](/getting-started/beta/).
- **The day you joined** is kept, to number your weeks in the beta.

Untick the box to leave. The flags go back to the build's default and
updates follow stable releases again. The app never installs an older
version, so you keep the current one until a stable release passes it.

## Feedback

The same panel has a short form: what kind (*something is broken*, *an
idea*, *a question*), which part of the app, a title and the text.
**Open feedback on GitHub** opens a new tab with a GitHub issue filled in
and labelled `beta-feedback`. Nothing is sent until you submit it there.
Lumen has no feedback server.

If the text is too long for a link, it is copied for you to paste into
the issue. Whether the app version, platform and language go in is your
choice.

## The weekly report (a second opt-in)

Tick **Once a week, prepare a usage report I can send**. It is off by
default and only offered to testers who joined. Once a week a reminder
appears, and the panel shows the whole report before anything leaves.

What is in it is the [usage report](/security/usage-metrics/), counts only,
plus three fields:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `cohort` | The Monday of the week you joined |
| `weeksInBeta` | Whole weeks since you joined |
| `channel` | `beta` or `stable` (the update channel) |

Days used, starts, errors and the app's own command names. No notes,
names, ids or time of day. **Open report on GitHub** opens an issue
labelled `beta-report` with the report as JSON. **Copy report** puts the
same text on the clipboard. Either way is recorded in the privacy log.

## How the reports are read

The project reads only the reports testers chose to send. The script
`npm run beta:funnel` reads the `beta-report` issues, or a folder of saved
reports, and counts the funnel:

- **Joined:** cohorts seen in any report.
- **Reported:** sent at least one report.
- **Active:** used Lumen on 3 or more of the 7 days, in some week.
- **Active 7 days:** used Lumen on all 7 days of a week.
- **Retained:** came back after a week (`retained7`).

A tester who never sends a report is not counted. That is the price of
not tracking anyone.

## The unmoderated usability tests

Twelve self-guided sessions run in Lumen's own test mode (Command palette
→ **Usability test (self-guided)…**, from the unmoderated round, #487),
with the tasks and the SUS questionnaire in Hebrew. The protocol is in
`research/usability/` in the repository. The tester sends the results by
hand, as with the reports, and `scripts/usability-analyze.mjs` reads them.
The beta funnel and the usability analysis are separate: neither joins the
other's data.

The script npm run beta:funnel reads the beta-report issues, or a folder of saved reports, and counts the funnel: Joined: cohorts seen in any report. Reported: sent at least one report. Active: used Lumen on 3 or more of the 7 days, in some week. Active 7 days: used Lumen on all 7 days of a week. Retained: came back after a week (retained7). A tester who never sends a report is not counted. That is the price of not tracking anyone.

pages.md:
Lumen is built in the open, in Hebrew and English.

## The beta

- **Joining:** open a discussion in the **Beta** category of the project's
  GitHub Discussions. It's a short form, and you need a GitHub account.
  The beta page (`/beta.html`) explains it all and sends nothing by itself.
- **What you get:** new features before everyone else. They ship behind
  feature flags in beta builds first.
- **What we ask:** use Lumen for real writing a few times a week, and tell
  us what got in the way, in **Beta feedback**.
- **The weekly survey:** a short, voluntary poll, *how many days this week
  did you open Lumen?* It is the only way we count testers. Lumen has no
  analytics and doesn't count you.
- **Keep a backup:** *Export the whole vault* now and then. It's a beta.

## Where to talk

| For | Where |
|---|---|
| Beta feedback: bugs, ideas, Hebrew and RTL problems | Discussions → *Beta feedback* |
| A confirmed bug or a concrete feature | GitHub Issues |
| Questions, show and tell | Discussions → *Q&A*, *Show and tell* |
| Security problems | privately, as in `SECURITY.md` |

Hebrew or English, whichever you prefer.

## The code of conduct

The project follows the
[Contributor Covenant 2.1](https://www.contributor-covenant.org/version/2/1/code_of_conduct.html).
The repository has it in English (`CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md`) and in Hebrew
(`CODE_OF_CONDUCT.he.md`). In short:

- assume good intent;
- criticise the work, not the person;
- no harassment, no personal attacks, no sharing others' private
  information.

Reports go privately to the maintainers, as described in `COMMUNITY.md`,
and are kept confidential.

## How Lumen compares

The [comparison page](/project/compare/) puts Lumen next to Obsidian, Notion
and Google Docs on five points, with a source for every claim and a list of
what Lumen still lacks.

pages.description: An honest comparison for people who write in Hebrew: what each one does, with a source for every claim, and what Lumen still lacks.
pages.md:
Each one is good at something. This page says what each does on five points that matter when you write in Hebrew, and every claim links to where it can be checked. Claims about the other products come from their own pages.

## Price

| | What it does | Sources |
|---|---|---|
| **Lumen** | Free. In the browser there is nothing to install, and notes stay in the browser's private storage. | [Lumen docs](/getting-started/install/) · <https://github.com/talstilkol/lumen-md/blob/main/LICENSE> (Checked 2026-11-10) |
| **Obsidian** | Free, for personal use and, since February 2025, for work too. Sync is a paid add-on ($4 a month, billed yearly). | <https://obsidian.md/blog/free-for-work/> · <https://obsidian.md/pricing.html> (Checked 2026-11-10) |
| **Notion** | A free plan, and paid plans: Plus, Business and Enterprise. | <https://www.notion.com/pricing> (Checked 2026-11-15) |
| **Google Docs** | — Not stated: this claim has not been checked against the maker's own page yet, so it is not shown. | <https://workspace.google.com/pricing> (⚠ not yet verified) |

## Hebrew and right-to-left

| | What it does | Sources |
|---|---|---|
| **Lumen** | Interface in Hebrew with a mirrored layout; direction per line; search that ignores niqqud and Hebrew prefixes. | [Lumen docs](/editor/hebrew/) (Checked 2026-11-10) |
| **Obsidian** | Since version 1.6: a mirrored interface for right-to-left languages, Hebrew among them, and notes in RTL, LTR or both. | <https://docs.obsidian.md/Plugins/User+interface/Right-to-left> (Checked 2026-11-10) |
| **Notion** | Interface in Hebrew, mirrored in the desktop and mobile apps; text direction detected in most blocks, but not in simple tables. | <https://www.notion.com/help/change-your-language> (Checked 2026-11-10) |
| **Google Docs** | Right-to-left controls turn on for documents with RTL text; paragraph direction and table column order can be set. | <https://support.google.com/docs/answer/65166> (Checked 2026-11-10) |

| | What it does | Sources |
|---|---|---|
| **Lumen** | The installed web app opens and works without a network; notes are stored on the device. | [Lumen docs](/getting-started/install/) (Checked 2026-11-10) |
| **Obsidian** | Notes are plain-text Markdown files in a vault, a folder on the device's file system, so they open without a network. | <https://obsidian.md/help/data-storage> (Checked 2026-11-15) |
| **Notion** | Since August 2025, offline in the desktop and mobile apps (not the browser): downloaded pages, plus Recents and Favorites on Plus, Business and Enterprise. | <https://www.notion.com/releases/2025-08-19> (Checked 2026-11-10) |
| **Google Docs** | — Not stated: this claim has not been checked against the maker's own page yet, so it is not shown. | <https://support.google.com/docs/answer/6388102> (⚠ not yet verified) |

## Markdown files

| | What it does | Sources |
|---|---|---|
| **Lumen** | Every note is a plain Markdown file; the whole vault exports as a .zip or a folder. | [Lumen docs](/workspace/export-import/) (Checked 2026-11-10) |
| **Obsidian** | Notes are Markdown-formatted plain-text files. | <https://obsidian.md/help/data-storage> (Checked 2026-11-15) |
| **Notion** | Any non-database page can be exported as Markdown; a whole workspace as HTML, Markdown or CSV (for databases). | <https://www.notion.com/help/export-your-content> (Checked 2026-11-15) |
| **Google Docs** | Since July 2024, import Markdown as a Doc and export a Doc as Markdown. | <https://workspaceupdates.googleblog.com/2024/07/import-and-export-markdown-in-google-docs.html> (Checked 2026-11-10) |

## Source code

| | What it does | Sources |
|---|---|---|
| **Lumen** | Open source under the MIT licence. | <https://github.com/talstilkol/lumen-md/blob/main/LICENSE> (Checked 2026-11-10) |
| **Obsidian** | Proprietary: Obsidian reserves the rights to the code in the app. The app is free for every use. | <https://obsidian.md/license> (Checked 2026-11-15) |

pages.title: Issue triage
pages.description: How new GitHub issues are labelled, checked for duplicates and linked to the plan within 24 hours.
pages.md:
Every new issue on [talstilkol/lumen-md](https://github.com/talstilkol/lumen-md/issues)
is looked at by a script within 24 hours, and a person reads it as well. The
script is `scripts/issue-triage.mjs`; the workflow `.github/workflows/issue-triage.yml`
runs it when an issue is opened or reopened and once a day at 06:23 UTC.

## What an issue gets

| What | When | Label |
|---|---|---|
| Kind | from words in the title and body (English and Hebrew) | `bug`, `enhancement`, `question` or `documentation` |
| Area | up to two, the ones whose words appear most | `area:editor`, `area:hebrew`, `area:ai`, `area:storage`, … |
| Possible duplicate | another issue, open or closed, has a near-identical title | `duplicate?` |
| Reproduction request | a bug with no steps, browser or version | `needs-repro` |
| Plan task | a task number in the text (for example `4.5`), else the plan task whose title shares the most words | — (in the comment) |
| Done | always | `triaged` |

When there is something to say (a possible duplicate, missing steps, a plan
task) the script leaves **one** comment, in English and Hebrew. It finds its
own comment again by a hidden marker, so a rerun never comments twice. Labels
that do not exist yet are created.

## What it does not do

- It never closes, assigns or edits an issue, and never removes a label.
- Issue text is only matched against word lists: it is not executed and not
  sent anywhere. The script talks to GitHub's REST API through `gh` with the
  workflow's own token (`issues: write`) and nothing else.

## The daily report

The daily run writes a report — the issues of the last 24 hours with the labels,
duplicate and plan task each got — to the job summary and as the artifact
`reports-issue-triage`. Any open issue older than 24 hours that still has no
`triaged` label is listed and **fails the run**, so the 24-hour promise is
checked every day.

## Running it yourself

```bash
node scripts/issue-triage.mjs                 # dry run: prints what it would do
node scripts/issue-triage.mjs --apply         # writes labels and comments
node scripts/issue-triage.mjs --json out.json # the report as JSON too
```

A dry run needs only a logged-in `gh`; `--apply` needs write access to issues.

pages.title: Checking Lumen against Obsidian
pages.description: The owner's checklist for opening a vault Lumen saved in the real Obsidian (1.15 or later) and comparing every Bases view, row by row.
pages.md:
Lumen's tests read real vaults: ten public ones, pinned to a commit, with
their licences checked. Three of them were written by Obsidian 1.14–1.15.
The tests can't run Obsidian itself, though. This checklist does, on a Mac
with Obsidian installed. It takes about 20 minutes.

## What Obsidian 1.14–1.15 changed in files

From Obsidian's changelog (1.14.4 to 1.15.1), and what Lumen does with each:

| Change | Lumen |
|---|---|
| `groupOrder:` on a grouped view: the groups to show, in order; an empty item is "no value" | Shown in that order, and groups not listed are hidden, as the Bases reference says. A `groupOrder` that is not a list is ignored (the 1.14.4 fix). |
| Filters reordered by dragging, and moved between *All views* and *This view* | `moveFilter()` writes both. The rest of the file, comments included, is unchanged. Reordering and moving back gives the original bytes. |
| A filter value with `"` or `\` is saved escaped (1.15.0 fix) | Read as written. Lumen writes such a value the same way (`basesTextLiteral()`). |
| View keys the app writes: `columnSize`, `columnWidth`, `imageFit`, `imageAspectRatio`, `enableSearch`, `rowHeight` | Kept as written. |
| Long generated formulas (the TaskNotes plugin writes one of 2,384 characters) | Bases expressions may be up to 8,000 characters. The evaluation budget is unchanged. |
| Canvas, callouts | No file-format change in 1.15 (performance and display fixes only). |

## The checklist

1. **Make a vault Lumen saved.** Copy one of the corpus vaults
   (`src/__tests__/fixtures/obsidian-corpus/<vault>`) to a new folder and
   open that folder in Lumen. Then, in Lumen:
   - sort one view by clicking a column header;
   - edit one property of a note;
   - save one canvas;
   - save, and close Lumen.
2. **Write the probes:**
   `npm run obsidian:compare -- prepare <folder>`
   This writes one probe `.base` per view, beside each base, and installs
   the small *Lumen compare* plugin into `<folder>/.obsidian/plugins/`.
3. **Open the folder in Obsidian** (1.15.1 or later): *Open folder as
   vault*. Settings → Community plugins → turn on *Lumen compare*.
4. **Watch for warnings while it opens.** Note any notice about a `.base`
   or `.canvas` file, or about properties. There should be none.
5. **Run the probes:** command palette → *Lumen compare: Run every probe*.
   Obsidian opens each probe in turn, then each original `.base` and
   `.canvas`, and saves what it showed into `_lumen-compare/results/`.
   Wait for the notice that ends with "files opened cleanly".
6. **Compare:**
   `npm run obsidian:compare -- diff <folder> --out obsidian-diff.md`
   The report lists every view as ✅ (the same rows), ↕ (the same rows in
   another order, in a view that sorts or groups), ❌ (different rows, with
   the paths) or ⏳ (no result from Obsidian). It also lists the files
   Obsidian opened cleanly. It exits 1 if any view is ❌ or ⏳.
7. **Clean up:** `npm run obsidian:compare -- clean <folder>`
8. **Report:** attach `obsidian-diff.md` to the plan task (W6.34), and open
   an issue for each ❌ with its two path lists.

## How the comparison is fair

- Each probe sits beside its base, so `this.file`, its folder and links
  resolve the same in both apps.
- Lumen's side runs on the same files on disk, probes included, with their
  real sizes and times.
- Order is compared only where the view sorts or groups. Elsewhere neither
  app promises an order.
- The plugin uses the public Bases view API (`registerBasesView`). It makes
  no request and writes only inside `_lumen-compare/`.

pages.title: Owner session command
pages.description: One command per owner session. It prints exactly what to do in the browser, runs the commands for you after asking, verifies the result through the APIs, records a signed receipt per step and resumes where you stopped.
pages.md:
Plan W6.20. The [owner sessions](/project/owner-sessions/) as a command:

```bash
npm run owner:session -- accounts    # session 1: accounts, keys and switches (any computer)
npm run owner:session -- gpu         # session 2: models and data (the cloud GPU, the Mac as fallback)
npm run owner:session -- devices     # session 3: devices, releases and the merge
npm run owner:session -- status      # what is done, estimated against actual minutes
npm run owner:session -- check       # only the automatic checks: no prompts, nothing recorded
npm run owner:session -- collect     # every owner command in the open PRs, deduplicated and assigned
```

Each step works like this:

1. It prints what you do, with the exact page to open.
2. It offers its commands (for example `gh label create …`, or the Vercel setting) and runs each one only after you answer yes. `--yes` runs them without asking.
3. When you press Enter, it checks the result:
   - automatically where an API, a file or a command can tell: GitHub through `gh api`, Vercel's REST API with your `VERCEL_TOKEN`, Hugging Face, BrowserStack, Kaggle, `wrangler`, `gcloud`, ssh or `oci` to the factory VM, the release on GitHub
   - by asking you yes or no where only your eyes can tell. That answer is recorded as attested.
4. It writes a signed receipt for the step.

A step with an open check is recorded as open. The next run starts again at that step and adds the minutes. A finished step is skipped (`--redo <step>` runs it again). Hebrew: `--lang he`, or a Hebrew `LANG`.

## The steps

14 owner items in three sessions (plan W6.20 asks for at most 15). Every step has at least one automatic check: 41 automatic checks and 18 yes/no answers.

| Step | Min | What | Automatic checks | Your yes/no |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `accounts/github` | 15 | Merge #432, turn on GitHub's protections and Vercel's Ignored Build Step (W6.10, W6.12) | merged-432, label, private-vulnerability-reporting, secret-scanning, ignored-build-step | — |
| `accounts/vercel-hf` | 15 | Leaked VITE_ keys (15.18), the Hugging Face token and seed, dataset terms | no-secret-vite, hf-token, golden-seed, flores-terms | common-voice-terms |
| `accounts/signing` | 20 | Signing accounts and keys (store verification takes days: start it now) | updater-key, release-key, android-keystore, asc-key | apple-enrolled, play-console, windows-signing |
| `accounts/test-clouds` | 15 | Free test clouds: BrowserStack (Safari, iOS), Firebase Test Lab (Android), Kaggle (GPU) | browserstack, firebase, kaggle | — |
| `accounts/hosts` | 20 | Hosts: Cloudflare Pages + the model mirror, Fly signaling + the relay | wrangler, pages-project, pages-live, mirror-env, signaling, relay-env | — |
| `accounts/factory` | 25 | The verification factory on Oracle's free VM | vm-timer, receipts-repo, first-status | — |
| `gpu/models-day` | 20 | The real models day on Kaggle's free GPU (the Mac only as fallback), with the held-out sets | heldout-key, eval-branch | — |
| `gpu/golden` | 60 | Your part of the golden sets (an hour now, the rest over days) | recordings | text-sets, image-ratings |
| `gpu/archives` | 30 | Your own archives and libraries: mail, chats, Zotero | zotero-key | mail, chats, zotero |
| `gpu/cargo-zip` | 20 | The critical Cargo zip advisory and the npm updates that need a real install | zip-9, known-bad | — |
| `devices/manual-checks` | 60 | What only eyes and hands can check: Safari, Word, the phone, screen readers | safari-receipt | safari-checklist, word-rtl, share-sheet, phone, screen-readers |
| `devices/desktop-release` | 60 | Desktop: the native build, beta.1 and the update drill to beta.2, the store packages, the privacy audit | beta1, beta2, bundle, privacy-audit | update-drill, packages |
| `devices/mobile` | 45 | Mobile: signed Android and iOS builds to internal testing, and a Firebase robo run | aab, robo | internal-testing |
| `devices/live-and-merge` | 25 | Merge the trains last, then check the live site and ask for a re-crawl | train-merged, security-md, live-meta | recrawl |

Session 1 is estimated at 110 minutes. The step's real time goes into its receipt, and `status` shows the two side by side.

## What the checks need

Set these in the shell that runs the command. A check that is missing its token prints "cannot check" and leaves the step open. It is never counted as passed.

| Variable or tool | For |
|---|---|
| `gh auth login` | the GitHub checks and switches |
| `VERCEL_TOKEN` (vercel.com → Account Settings → Tokens; optional `VERCEL_TEAM_ID`, `VERCEL_PROJECT`) | the Ignored Build Step, the environment variables |
| `HF_TOKEN` | the FLORES+ terms (a gated file downloads) |
| `BROWSERSTACK_USERNAME`, `BROWSERSTACK_ACCESS_KEY` | BrowserStack Automate |
| `~/.kaggle/kaggle.json` (mode 600) or `KAGGLE_USERNAME` + `KAGGLE_KEY` | Kaggle |
| `gcloud`, `npx wrangler@4`, `cargo` | Firebase Test Lab, Cloudflare, the zip advisory |
| `LUMEN_FACTORY_VM=ubuntu@<ip>` (ssh), or `oci` + `OCI_COMPARTMENT` | the factory's nightly timer |
| `LUMEN_GOLDEN_DIR`, `ZOTERO_API_KEY` | the recordings count, the Zotero key |

## Receipts

Each step writes `reports/owner/<session>/<step>.json` in the sealed format of the nightly receipts and the plan's receipt reader: canonical JSON, sha256 and an Ed25519 signature.

- The receipt holds the commit you ran on, the start and finish times, the estimated and actual minutes, each command's exit code, and each check's result (attested answers are marked).
- The key is made on the first run at `~/.config/lumen-md/owner-ed25519.pem` (mode 600; `LUMEN_OWNER_KEY` overrides). Its public half is `reports/owner/PUBLIC_KEY.pem`.
- A receipt changed by hand no longer verifies and is ignored.
- At the end, the command prints the `git add -f reports/owner …` line that commits the receipts.

The works-for-the-user board (plan W6.44) reads them. For example, `accounts/github` → `secret-scanning` is evidence for privacy and security.

## Collecting owner commands

`collect` reads the owner sections of every open PR:
- the headings it reads are "Owner commands", "Owner steps", "Owner items" and "The owner's … step"
- each command is a line in a shell block, an inline command, or a to-do bullet
- it merges duplicates across PRs and assigns each one

Each command goes to one of these:

| Assigned to | Meaning |
|---|---|
| a step | the step that takes care of it |
| agent | a test or build run that agents do on the second host |
| recurring | a loop per train or merge (pr:check, restack, train builds) |
| coordinator | a change a lane makes in a PR |
| people | needs other people (raters, speakers, a second maintainer) |
| deferred | optional and deferred (15.5) |
| obsolete | a GitHub Actions run (the project doesn't use Actions) |
| none | the section says nothing is needed |

An unassigned command, or a plan owner item (15.x) that no step carries and that isn't listed as taken off, makes `collect` exit 1. A new owner command can't be missed that way. `collect --write` saves the result as `scripts/owner/inbox.json`.

On 12.11.2026: 375 open PRs, 79 with an owner section, 236 distinct items:
- 149 in the 14 steps
- 58 for agents
- 20 recurring
- 4 for the coordinator
- 2 needing other people
- 1 deferred, 1 obsolete, 1 "none"
- 0 unassigned

All 18 plan owner items are covered: 13 in steps and 5 taken off the list.

**Run it as a command:** `npm run owner:session -- accounts|gpu|devices` prints each step, runs and verifies it, and records a signed receipt ([Owner session command](/project/owner-session-command/), plan W6.20). It regroups the items below into 14 steps.

Plan W4.7. Gathered 12.11.2026 from `plan.json` → `owner` (15.1–15.18) and the
"## Owner commands" sections of all 300 open pull requests (37 have one).
Every item is either here, with its time and command, or listed under
"Taken off the owner's list" with who does it instead.

**Order:** Session 1 (accounts) first — store verification takes days and
several later steps need its tokens. Session 2 (GPU Mac) and session 3
(devices) can then go in either order. 15.1 (merging) comes last.

Commands that come with an open pull request are written as the script they run (the PR is named next to them), so they work on that PR's branch before it is merged: `node scripts/models-day.mjs` is #443's `models:day`, `bash scripts/pages-deploy.sh` is #484's `pages:deploy`.

## The count

|---|---|---|

pages.title: Open PR triage
pages.description: One decision table for every open pull request — in main, in a train, superseded, dependabot, or still needed — and the commands that close each category with a comment.
pages.md:
Most pull requests here are stacked: each one is built on the branch of the
one before. When a train (`verify/train`, `verify/train-2`, …) is merged, GitHub
does not mark the PRs inside it as merged, so they stay open. 356 open PRs
hide the few that are really open work (plan W6.21).

`scripts/pr-triage.mjs` sorts every open PR into one category, so the owner
approves a **category** once instead of each PR:

| Category | Rule | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| `in-main` | `git merge-base --is-ancestor <head> origin/main`: every commit of the PR is in main | Close now, with a comment |
| `in-train` | the head is an ancestor of a train (`verify/train`, `verify/train-2`, `verify/train-3`) but not of main | Close once that train is promoted to main: it then becomes `in-main` |
| `superseded` | a later PR says "Supersedes #N" (or "Replaces" / "Obsoletes"), or a later PR of the same plan task contains every commit of this one | Close with the reason, after the owner reads the list |
| `dependabot` | opened by dependabot | Lane S triages them in the dependency train (W6.14) |
| `train` | the head is `verify/*`: the train itself | Merged or closed with the promotion, by hand |
| `needed` | anything else | Stays open |

The order matters: a PR is put in the first category that fits.

## What it does not do

- It never closes anything unless it is run with `--close <category> --go`, and
  then only `in-main` or `superseded`. An `in-train` PR is closed only after its
  train is in main, because the close step re-checks main.
- It never deletes a branch. A closed PR's branch is kept for 30 days, so the PR
  can be reopened.
- A PR whose commits reached a train only after a rebase or squash has a
  different head, so it counts as `needed`, not contained. The script errs
  towards keeping a PR open.
- PR titles and bodies are matched against patterns; they are never executed.

## Running it

```sh
node scripts/pr-triage.mjs                    # the table, nothing written
node scripts/pr-triage.mjs --write            # also rewrites the generated part below (and the Hebrew page)
node scripts/pr-triage.mjs --json rows.json   # every row as JSON
node scripts/pr-triage.mjs --close in-main    # what it would close (dry run)
node scripts/pr-triage.mjs --close in-main --go
```

It needs `gh` signed in and a clone with full history (a shallow clone cannot
answer "is this an ancestor?"); `--git-dir <path>` points at another clone, for
example `git clone --bare --filter=tree:0 …`, which has every commit but no
files. Run it after every promotion of main.

sections.text: Most pull requests here are stacked: each one is built on the branch of the one before. When a train (verify/train, verify/train-2, …) is merged, GitHub does not mark the PRs inside it as merged, so they stay open. 356 open PRs hide the few that are really open work (plan W6.21). scripts/pr-triage.mjs sorts every open PR into one category, so the owner approves a category once instead of each PR: Category Rule What happens --- --- --- in-main git merge-base --is-ancestor origin/main: every commit of the PR is in main Close now, with a comment in-train the head is an ancestor of a train (verify/train, verify/train-2, verify/train-3) but not of main Close once that train is promoted to main: it then becomes in-main superseded a later PR says "Supersedes #N" (or "Replaces" / "Obsoletes"), or a later PR of the same plan task contains every commit of this one Close with the reason, after the owner reads the list dependabot opened by dependabot Lane S triages them in the dependency train (W6.14) train the head is verify/ : the train itself Merged or closed with the promotion, by hand needed anything else Stays open The order matters: a PR is put in the first category that fits.

sections.heading: What it does not do
sections.text: It never closes anything unless it is run with --close --go, and then only in-main or superseded. pages.title: Pricing
pages.description: Lumen is free and MIT-licensed forever, with no account. The only paid things are optional — an encrypted sync relay at $4 a month and a one-time supporter payment — and the free tier never shrinks.
pages.md:
## The app: free, forever

- **Free, with every feature.** Nothing in the app is locked behind a payment.
- **MIT licence.** The code is yours to read, run, change and share ([LICENSE](https://github.com/talstilkol/lumen-md/blob/main/LICENSE)).
- **No account.** Your notes stay on your device as Markdown files.
- **The free tier never shrinks.** No feature that is free today will become paid. This promise is also in the README.
- **Only hosted services can be paid.** In the code, `src/billing/gates.ts` may gate only a service that runs on a server and costs money (the encrypted relay, hosted publish, the persistent collaboration server). Search, semantic search, AI with your own key or a local model, and the number of devices are never limited, even when an operator turns billing on. A test lists every gate and fails if a local feature is among them.

Sync between your devices is free too, through your own relay (`node sync-server/vault-relay.js`), a folder you already sync, or Git.

## Optional: the encrypted sync relay

For people who would rather not run a relay themselves. The relay sees only encrypted data: notes are encrypted on the device before they leave it ([Sustainability](/project/sustainability/) explains what the relay can and can't see).

| Plan | Price |
| --- | --- |
| Monthly | **$4** a month |
| Yearly | **$40** a year (ten months) |

<button type="button" disabled data-pay="relay-monthly">Subscribe monthly ($4)</button>
<button type="button" disabled data-pay="relay-yearly">Subscribe yearly ($40)</button>

## Optional: support Lumen once

A one-time payment of about **$25**, for people who want to support the work. It unlocks nothing, because there is nothing to unlock.

<button type="button" disabled data-pay="supporter">Support once ($25)</button>

## Discounts and free use

- **Students and teachers:** 50% off the relay.
- **Schools, yeshivas and nonprofits:** the relay is free.

## Payments are not open yet

The buttons above are disabled. Payments open only once the payment provider is set up (plan W11.O8). Until then nothing on this page can take a payment. Donations are open now: [Sustainability](/project/sustainability/).

pages.title: Releasing a version
pages.description: One local command builds, signs and checks a release, and with --publish puts it on GitHub Releases with signed desktop updates. No GitHub Actions.
pages.md:
A release is one command on the release owner's computer. GitHub Actions
are not needed.

```bash
npm run release -- 0.2.0-beta.1 --dry-run     # build, sign and check everything; publish nothing
npm run release -- 0.2.0-beta.1 --publish     # the owner: commit, tag, build, sign, push, GitHub release
```

A dry run puts the tree back when it finishes: the version, `CHANGELOG.md` and
`src-tauri/tauri.conf.json` return to what they were. It leaves `release/`
with every asset, plus `release/DRY-RUN.md`, which lists the assets and the
exact commands `--publish` would run.

## What the command does

1. **Preflight.** It lists everything that is missing (a key, a tool, the
   release notes, a clean tree, the `main` branch, `gh auth`), each with the
   command that fixes it. A dry run needs no key. A publish needs every one.
2. **Version and changelog.** It bumps the version in `package.json`,
   `package-lock.json`, `tauri.conf.json`, `Cargo.toml` and the iOS project.
   It writes the `CHANGELOG.md` section from the pull requests merged since
   the last tag: one line per PR, sorted by the type in its title (Added,
   Fixed, Performance, …), with a link to the PR. PR titles come from the
   GitHub API; offline (`--offline`) it uses the merge commits.
3. **Commit and tag** (`--publish` only): `chore(release): X` and `vX`.
4. **The updater.** The committed `tauri.conf.json` carries the placeholder
   `${LUMEN_UPDATER_PUBKEY}`. The release fills in the public key and the
   endpoint on GitHub Releases (stable: `releases/latest/download/latest.json`;
   a beta: the rolling `beta-channel` release). It also turns on signed update
   bundles. The build stops if the key is empty, is still the placeholder or
   is not a minisign key. Afterwards the file goes back to the placeholder.
   The separate `node scripts/release.mjs publish` refuses as well: with the
   placeholder, an empty key, the throwaway test key or a fake build in
   `release/`, it stops before any `git` or `gh` command.
5. **A reproducible web build.** `repro-check` builds twice with
   `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` and compares every file, then the bundle budget and the
   source-map check run. `lumen-web-vX.tgz` is the same bytes on every machine:
   the files are sorted, the owner and mode are fixed, and the gzip header has
   no time.
6. **Desktop.** `tauri build` runs with `TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY`. The macOS
   update bundle gets its version and architecture in its name.
   `latest.json` is built from the `.sig` files. Every signature is checked
   against the updater key, and the same check must refuse a copy with one
   byte changed.
   `latest.json` itself is then signed with the same updater key
   (`latest.json.sig`, the same format as a bundle's `.sig`). The run checks
   that signature, and a copy with one byte changed must be refused. **The
   run refuses to publish without it**: the app downloads `latest.json` and
   `latest.json.sig`, verifies the signature before it reads anything in the
   manifest, and refuses a version that isn't newer than the running one and
   the highest ever installed (W11.S2/S3). With the owner's key the signing
   is `tauri signer sign` on the file.
   Under that signature `latest.json` also names its `channel` (`stable`, or
   `beta` for the `beta-channel` copy) and an `expires` time 90 days ahead.
   The app refuses a manifest for another channel than the feed it read, and
   one past its expiry, so an old manifest served again can't hold updates
   back for longer than that: release (or re-run the beta channel) at least
   every 90 days. Before the beta channel merges and re-signs the
   `latest.json` already on the `beta-channel` release, it checks that file's
   own `latest.json.sig`; one that doesn't verify is not merged, and the
   channel is rebuilt from this release alone.
7. **SBOM.** `sbom.cdx.json` (CycloneDX 1.5) lists every package in
   `package-lock.json` and every crate in `Cargo.lock`. It is built offline.
8. **Release notes.** Hebrew first, then English, from
   `release-notes/<version>.he.md` and `release-notes/<version>.en.md`
   (written by hand, a few lines each), then the full change list and how to
   verify the download.
9. **Checksums.** `SHA256SUMS` lists every asset. It is signed with minisign
   (`SHA256SUMS.minisig`), and so is the SBOM. The whole folder is then
   verified, and a changed `SHA256SUMS` must fail.
   Then the provenance gate runs ([Build provenance and Sigstore signatures](/security/provenance/)):
   - SLSA provenance over the exact files, signed with the build key
   - a keyless Sigstore bundle per file, from Tal's login
   - `verify.mjs` checks both for every file; nothing is pushed unless it passes

   A dry run uses TEST keys and a local Sigstore stand-in instead.
10. **Publish** (`--publish` only): `git push origin HEAD vX`, then
    `gh release create`. A beta is a pre-release and is never "latest", so
    stable users never get it. Then `latest.json` is uploaded to the
    `beta-channel` release.

## Options

| Option | What it does |
|---|---|
| `--dry-run` | the default: nothing is committed, tagged or published |
| `--publish` | the real release (the owner) |
| `--fake-build` | dry run only: stand-in bundles where `node_modules`, Rust or the Tauri CLI are missing; every later step still runs. A publish refuses it. |
| `--no-repro` | one web build instead of two |
| `--no-desktop` | web, SBOM and checksums only |
| `--skip-checks` | no typecheck and no tests before the build |
| `--offline` | PR titles from git, not from the GitHub API |

## Keys (made once, kept by the owner)

| Key | Made with | Used through |
|---|---|---|
| Updater signing key | `npx tauri signer generate -w ~/.tauri/lumen-updater.key` | `TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY` (+ `TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD`) |
| Updater public key | written next to it (`.key.pub`) | commit it as `security/updater-key.pub`, or set `LUMEN_UPDATER_PUBKEY` |
| Release key (checksums, SBOM) | `node scripts/supply-chain/keys.mjs` | `LUMEN_RELEASE_KEY` (+ `LUMEN_RELEASE_PASSPHRASE`); commit `security/release-key.pub` |

When a key is missing, a dry run signs with throwaway test keys and says so.
Their public keys have `TEST` in their comment line, and a publish refuses
them.

## Checking a release (anyone)

```bash
gh release download v0.2.0-beta.1 --repo talstilkol/lumen-md --dir lumen
cd lumen && minisign -Vm SHA256SUMS -p release-key.pub && sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS
# or, without minisign:
node scripts/supply-chain/verify-release.mjs lumen --pub security/release-key.pub
```

## Limits

- One `--publish` run uploads the bundles of the machine it runs on: the
  macOS bundles from a Mac. Bundles for Linux and Windows from other
  machines are not added to the same release yet. Until they are, publish
  from the Mac (that gives at least the `.dmg`, the update bundle, its
  signature, the web `.tgz` and the SBOM).
- Rolling back is `node scripts/release.mjs rollback <bad> --to <good>` (see
  `RELEASE.md`).

Every Lumen deployment serves an open roadmap at `/roadmap.html` (and at
`/roadmap` on Cloudflare Pages, Netlify and the Docker image). The status bar's
**Roadmap** link opens it.

## Where it comes from

The page is the third output of `npm run plan`, next to the board in
`MASTER_PLAN.md` and `plan/board.html`. All three are rendered from one file,
`plan/plan.json`, and `npm run plan:check` fails CI when any of them differs
from it. So the roadmap changes in the same commit as the plan, every time.

## What it shows — and what it does not

| Shown | Not shown |
|---|---|
| every phase, with its number and title | the steps of a task and its acceptance line |
| every task's number and title | estimates, dates and the schedule |
| its state: **done** (✅), **in progress** (⏳) or **planned** | branches, PR numbers and the owner's items (phase 15) |
| the counts and a progress bar | anything from issues or notes |

The full plan, with every measured acceptance criterion, is in the repository.

## How it renders

`public/roadmap.html` carries the data as a JSON block; `public/roadmap.js`
builds the cards with `textContent`. The script is external because the app's
Content-Security-Policy allows no inline script, and it needs no Trusted Types
policy because it never writes HTML. The page is Hebrew and right-to-left,
laid out with logical CSS properties.

## Updating it

```bash
npm run plan        # rewrites MASTER_PLAN.md's board, plan/board.html and public/roadmap.html
npm run plan:check  # what CI runs: exit 1 when any of them is out of date
```
